summary.text: The chosen shift is \(k=0\). Since \(s(z)\) is defined as \(a(\max(z,0))\), every \(n\ge 0\) satisfies \(s(n+0)=a(n)\).

full_proof.text:
Define the height-dependent level-step weights \(b_k\) for \(k\in\mathbb N\) by
\[
b_0=1,
\]
and, for \(k\ge 1\), by
\[
b_k=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{k}{2}+1,&k\text{ is even},\\[4pt]
0,&k\text{ is odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the weights begin
\[
1,0,2,0,3,0,4,0,\ldots.
\]

Using these weights, define numbers \(A(n,k)\), for \(n,k\in\mathbb N\), recursively as follows. The initial values are
\[
A(0,0)=1,\qquad A(0,k)=0\quad(k>0),
\]
and the recurrence is
\[
A(n+1,k)
 =A(n,k+1)
 +\begin{cases}0,&k=0,\\ A(n,k-1),&k>0,\end{cases}
 +b_kA(n,k).
\]
Combinatorially, \(A(n,k)\) is the total weight of the Motzkin paths of length \(n\) from height \(0\) to height \(k\): the three terms in the recurrence account respectively for a final down-step from height \(k+1\), a final up-step from height \(k-1\) (which is impossible when \(k=0\)), and a final level-step at height \(k\), whose weight is \(b_k\). The generalized Bessel-number sequence in the statement is
\[
a(n)=A(n,0)\qquad(n\in\mathbb N).
\]

The integer-indexed sequence denoted by \(s\) in the statement is defined from this same sequence \(a\). For an integer \(z\), let
\[
z_{\mathbb N}=\begin{cases}
z,&z\ge 0,\\
0,&z<0,
\end{cases}
\]
where in the first case the nonnegative integer \(z\) is regarded as a natural number. Then
\[
s(z)=a(z_{\mathbb N}).
\]
In particular, for every natural number \(n\), viewed as a nonnegative integer, one has
\[
n_{\mathbb N}=n.
\]

We now exhibit the required integer shift. Take
\[
k=0.
\]
Let \(n\ge 0\) be arbitrary. Since adding zero does not change an integer and the integer corresponding to the natural number \(n\) is nonnegative,
\[
(n+k)_{\mathbb N}=(n+0)_{\mathbb N}=n_{\mathbb N}=n.
\]
Consequently, by the definition of \(s\),
\[
s(n+k)=a\bigl((n+k)_{\mathbb N}\bigr)=a(n).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a(n)=s(n+k).
\]
Because this holds for every \(n\in\mathbb N\), the integer \(k=0\) satisfies
\[
\forall n\ge 0,\qquad a(n)=s(n+k).
\]
Hence there exists an integer shift with the required property.
